\chapter{The Person, Head To Hand}
\label{ch:la-mujer-y-la-cara}
\hlchaptermodality{364}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say la mujer, la cara, la nariz, el dedo and el corazón, and point at a person and name a part of them.}

Complete ES-C364-corazon: name a person, then a face, a nose, a finger and the thing that beats underneath.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la mujer]{la mujer — the Latin woman-word English never took}

\label{lesson:ES-C364-mujer}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the bus}, then \emph{the bicycle}. (\emph{El autobús}; \emph{la bicicleta}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la persona — the general word for a human being, which this narrows.
  \item la esposa — the other way Spanish names a wife, and the contrast matters here.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mu-JER}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{j} is the jota, scraped at the back of the throat. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la mujer} — \textquotedblleft{}the woman.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had two everyday words for a human being, and they had very different luck. \textbf{Homō} meant a person, and it travelled everywhere: English \textbf{human}, \textbf{humane}, \textbf{homicide}, and \textbf{homage} — a man declaring himself another man's man — all descend from it, some through French, some lifted straight out of Latin by scholars. \textbf{Mulier} meant a woman, and it went almost nowhere.

Count what English got. There is \textbf{muliebrity}, \textquotedblleft{}womanhood\textquotedblright{}, whose earliest evidence is around 1592 and which never became common; \textbf{muliebral} is rarer still. That is close to the whole harvest. A word Romans used constantly, for half of everybody, left English an empty shelf.

Spanish kept it and wore it down: \emph{mulier} became \textbf{mujer}, the middle of the word hardening into that scraped jota. Portuguese, Catalan and Italian kept it too. French alone let it go, replacing it with \emph{femme}, from Latin \emph{fēmina}.

And where did \emph{mulier} itself come from? Nobody knows. The Romans guessed \textbf{mollior}, \textquotedblleft{}softer\textquotedblright{} — a tidy story, and wrong, because the sounds do not line up. A rival guess ties it to \emph{mulgēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to milk\textquotedblright{}, with no more support than the first. Modern handbooks print the word and leave the origin line blank, which is an honest thing for a dictionary to do.

One practical note. \textbf{Mujer} carries two senses at once, \textquotedblleft{}woman\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}wife\textquotedblright{}, and only the sentence around it tells you which one is meant.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name a human being and then narrow it: \emph{la persona}, \emph{la mujer}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la mujer}
  \item \emph{una mujer}
  \item \emph{la mujer de la casa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did English take from Latin \emph{mulier}? (Almost nothing — the rare word \emph{muliebrity}.) And where does \emph{mulier} itself come from? (Unexplained; the softer story is a Roman folk etymology.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la cara]{la cara — the face that is also expensive}

\label{lesson:ES-C364-cara}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the bicycle}, then \emph{the woman}. (\emph{La bicicleta}; \emph{la mujer}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el ojo — one of the parts this word gathers together.
  \item la boca — the other part already named, which sits in the same place.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CA-ra}, two beats with the weight on the first. The single \emph{r} is a quick tap, the tongue brushing the ridge behind the teeth once. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la cara} — \textquotedblleft{}the face.\textquotedblright{}

Begin with the half that is solid. Spanish has two words with this exact shape, and they have nothing to do with each other.

The second one is an adjective. \textbf{Caro} means \textquotedblleft{}expensive\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \textbf{cārus}, \textquotedblleft{}dear\textquotedblright{} — dear in both English senses, costly and beloved. That root was generous to English: \textbf{charity} is \emph{cāritās}, dearness; \textbf{cherish} comes through Old French \emph{cherir}; \textbf{caress} arrives from Italian \emph{carezza} by way of French. Say the adjective first and you get \emph{una cara cara}, an expensive face, a phrase Spaniards actually use and a small proof that the two words run independently. The same noun gives \emph{cara o cruz}, the Spanish way of saying heads or tails.

Now the noun, and here the ground goes soft. Late Latin \textbf{cara} \textquotedblleft{}face\textquotedblright{} is generally traced to Greek \textbf{kára}, \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{}. That is the majority account and it is worth carrying. It is also contested from inside the field: Corominas pointed out that \emph{kára} is a poetic word in Greek rather than a workaday one, that no secure trace of it turns up in the everyday Latin that fed Romance, and that the word surfaces in the wrong places across Romance for a Greek borrowing. So the honest version is this: usually derived from Greek \emph{kára}, with the trail broken somewhere in the middle.

A word you use fifty times a day, whose family tree carries a question mark — and a twin meaning \textquotedblleft{}costly\textquotedblright{} that is no relation at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name three things that sit together: \emph{el ojo}, \emph{la boca}, \emph{la cara}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cara}
  \item \emph{una cara}
  \item \emph{la cara de la mujer}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What else does \emph{cara} mean, and from which root? (Expensive, from Latin cārus — the root of charity and cherish.) And how firm is the Greek origin of the face-word? (It is the usual account, but the trail is not clean.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la nariz]{la nariz — the nostril word that swallowed the nose}

\label{lesson:ES-C364-nariz}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the woman}, then \emph{the face}. (\emph{La mujer}; \emph{la cara}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la boca — the neighbouring opening, already named.
  \item el oído — another opening in the head, and another word built on what it does.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{na-RIZ}, two beats with the weight on the second. In much of Spain that final \emph{z} is a soft th; across Latin America it is a clean \emph{s}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la nariz} — \textquotedblleft{}the nose.\textquotedblright{}

Latin kept the thing apart from its openings. \textbf{Nāsus} was the nose. \textbf{Nāris} was a nostril, and it mostly turned up in the plural, \textbf{nārēs}, since you have two of them. Spanish then did something unexpected with that pair: it held on to the nostril word and let the nose word go. \textbf{Nariz} is \emph{nāris}, its shape nudged along the way by \emph{nāsus} sitting close by.

The plural did not vanish either. Spanish still says \emph{meter las narices} for poking your nose into someone else's business — nostrils, plural, counted exactly as a Roman would have counted them. A two-thousand-year-old habit of number, preserved inside an idiom about being nosy.

English kept the other branch, and took it through two different doors. \textbf{Nose} was inherited: Old English \emph{nosu}, a Germanic cousin of \emph{nāsus}, not a loan from it — the two words came down side by side from one ancient source. \textbf{Nasal} is the loan, pulled out of Latin \emph{nāsālis} by writers who wanted a technical word. Then \textbf{nostril} is Old English \emph{nosthyrl}, a nose-hole, where only the first half is the cousin; the \emph{-thyrl} is kin to \textbf{through} and to \textbf{thrill}, which once meant to pierce. And \textbf{nozzle} is homegrown, a small English diminutive of \emph{nose}, with no Latin anywhere in it.

So English ended up with the nose. Spanish, strictly speaking, ended up with the nostrils.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name three openings in a head: \emph{la boca}, \emph{el oído}, \emph{la nariz}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la nariz}
  \item \emph{una nariz}
  \item \emph{la nariz y la boca}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word gave \emph{nariz}, and what did it mean? (Nāris, a nostril.) And what does \emph{meter las narices} preserve? (The Latin plural — nostrils rather than nose.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el dedo]{el dedo — the finger inside anything digital}

\label{lesson:ES-C364-dedo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the face}, then \emph{the nose}. (\emph{La cara}; \emph{la nariz}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la mano — where five of these live.
  \item el pie — where the other five live, since Spanish uses one word for both.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{DE-do}, two beats with the weight on the first. Both \emph{d}s are soft, the tongue barely touching, nearer the \emph{th} of \emph{this} than an English \emph{d}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el dedo} — \textquotedblleft{}the finger.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{digitus} covered fingers and toes with a single word, and Spanish inherited the arrangement: \emph{dedo} does both jobs, and you add a phrase when it matters which end of a person you mean.

The English side of the family took a detour through arithmetic. A \textbf{digit} began as a finger and became a numeral, for the plain reason that hands are the first counting device anyone owns — ten fingers are why the numerals run out at ten and start over. Once \emph{digit} had settled into \textquotedblleft{}numeral\textquotedblright{}, \textbf{digital} was built on that sense: discrete numbers, counted one at a time, as against a smoothly sliding quantity. So the word in \emph{digital camera} reaches you through counting, not through hands. Finger, then number, then machine — and the middle step is the one everybody forgets.

Two more relatives are worth having. \textbf{Prestidigitation}, a conjuror's sleight of hand, is \textquotedblleft{}quick-fingered\textquotedblright{}. And \textbf{digitalis}, the heart drug, is named for the foxglove, whose flowers are finger-shaped little tubes you could slip over a fingertip.

One collision to clear, because the shape invites it. Spanish \textbf{alrededor}, \textquotedblleft{}around\textquotedblright{}, appears to have a \emph{dedo} buried in the middle. It does not. That word is built on Latin \textbf{retrō}, \textquotedblleft{}backwards\textquotedblright{}; the sounds got shuffled on their way into Spanish and threw off a lookalike. Coincidence, not kinship.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name a hand, a foot, and what sticks out of both: \emph{la mano}, \emph{el pie}, \emph{el dedo}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el dedo}
  \item \emph{un dedo}
  \item \emph{los dedos de la mano}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \emph{digit} mean a numeral? (Because people count on their fingers.) And is \emph{alrededor} related to \emph{dedo}? (No — it is built on Latin retrō, backwards.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el corazón]{el corazón — the heart you bring things back to}

\label{lesson:ES-C364-corazon}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the nose}, then \emph{the finger}. (\emph{La nariz}; \emph{el dedo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el pecho — the part of the body this one sits inside.
  \item la sangre — what this organ moves, already named.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{co-ra-ZON}, three beats with the weight on the last, which is what the written accent marks. The single \emph{r} is one quick tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el corazón} — \textquotedblleft{}the heart.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{cor}, whose stem is \textbf{cord-}, is a short word that got everywhere. French kept it small as \emph{coeur}, Italian as \emph{cuore}. Spanish did something else: it hung an augmentative ending on it, the kind of ending that makes a thing bigger, and came away with \textbf{corazón} — a great heart where the neighbours kept a plain one.

English is thick with \emph{cord-}. \textbf{Cordial} is \textquotedblleft{}of the heart\textquotedblright{}, which slid from heartfelt to a warming drink you press on a guest. \textbf{Courage} is what your heart holds. \textbf{Accord} is two hearts brought together, \textbf{concord} the same, and \textbf{discord} is hearts pulled apart. But \textbf{record} is the pick of them. Latin \textbf{recordārī} meant to remember: \emph{re-} plus \emph{cor(d)-}, \textquotedblleft{}to bring back to the heart\textquotedblright{}, on the ancient view that memory lived in the chest rather than the skull. The later senses — a written record, a vinyl record, a world record — all grew out of \textquotedblleft{}a thing that helps you remember\textquotedblright{}.

And Spanish kept the original meaning. \textbf{Recordar} is still the plain daily verb for remembering, while English \emph{record} wandered off into filing cabinets and turntables.

Clear one collision before it catches you. That \emph{-razón} at the end is not the word \emph{razón}. \textbf{Razón} descends from Latin \emph{ratiō}, from \emph{rērī}, \textquotedblleft{}to reckon\textquotedblright{}, which also gave English \textbf{ratio}, \textbf{reason} and \textbf{rational}. What \emph{corazón} holds is \emph{cor} with an ending fastened on. The overlap is an accident of sound.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name what is under the skin and what moves through it: \emph{el pecho}, \emph{la sangre}, \emph{el corazón}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el corazón}
  \item \emph{un corazón}
  \item \emph{el corazón y la sangre}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{record} literally mean? (To bring a thing back to the heart.) And is \emph{corazón} made of \emph{co-} plus \emph{razón}? (No — it is \emph{cor} with a Spanish ending; \emph{razón} is a different root entirely.)
\end{tcolorbox}
